summary: Describes the services that the LSMA group found necessary for large-scale distributed simulation over multicast, and the aspects of the Internet protocols that need more development to meet those needs. It is informational and reads as a requirements and gaps document.

plainLanguage.summary: Lots of computers acting out a huge pretend world together need to send the same news to many places at once. This document lists what the internet can't yet do well for that.

questions: internet protocol gaps for large scale simulation
subtitle: What the internet can't yet do well for large-scale distributed simulation.

tldr.problem: The military and potentially commercial applications want to run large-scale distributed simulations (like DIS and HLA) with tens of thousands of objects across wide-area networks, but the Internet protocols have significant gaps.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC documents the requirements for large-scale simulation, then systematically identifies which Internet protocols and services are missing or inadequate to meet those needs.
tldr.outcome: The RFC informs the IETF about gaps that need to be addressed, including multicast scalability, resource reservation aggregation, ATM multicast support, reliable multicast, and session management protocols.

today: RFC 2502 is an Informational RFC that documents requirements and protocol gaps identified by the LSMA working group. It has informed subsequent protocol development and remains relevant for understanding the intersection of multicast, quality of service, and large-scale distributed systems.

sections.title: Large-Scale Distributed Simulation
sections.content:
The Large-Scale Multicast Applications (LSMA) working group was chartered to develop Internet protocols supporting large-scale multicast applications, including Distributed Interactive Simulation (DIS) and the High-Level Architecture for simulation (HLA).

In DIS, many computers simulate objects in a virtual environment and exchange state data in real time. Packets of about 2000 bits are sent at rates of 0.2 to 15 packets per second per simulator. The U.S. Department of Defense has a goal to build simulations with up to 100,000 objects. Maximum acceptable latency is around 100 milliseconds between any two hosts. Eventually such systems may support commercial entertainment applications.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine thousands of computers playing a game together where each one controls a tank or airplane in a pretend battle. All of them need to know where all the others are, right now, all the time.

sections.title: DIS and HLA Compared
sections.content:
DIS is an older protocol set where each simulator redundantly transmits object attribute updates, relying on best-effort transport (UDP). HLA is a newer approach with a Run Time Infrastructure (RTI) responsible for reliable transmission, potentially using a mix of redundant and reliable protocols.

DIS-like simulations require multicasting to send updates to all other simulators. HLA similarly requires many-to-many transmission of object data at rates exceeding one update per object per second. Both systems group hosts into multicast groups based on shared sensor inputs, potentially requiring thousands of groups. The aggregate data rate across all groups is bounded, but the rate within any individual group is unpredictable and changes rapidly.
sections.plainLanguage: In the older way (DIS), each computer sends the same message many times hoping everyone gets it. In the newer way (HLA), a special manager promises to deliver messages reliably, which could be more efficient if done right.

sections.title: Service Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC identifies six key requirements for LSMA networks:

  • Real-time packet delivery with low packet loss (under 2%), predictable latency of a few hundred milliseconds, and less than 2% of packets exceeding specified latency, in a shared network.
  • Multicasting supporting thousands of groups with join latencies under one second at rates of hundreds of joins per second.
  • Many-to-many multicast where 90% or more of group members are both senders and receivers.
  • Dynamic resource reservation so different groups can share reserved capacity.
  • Hybrid best-effort and reliable low-latency multicast, with best-effort predominating.
  • Secure networking with per-packet encryption and authentication for classified military simulations.
sections.plainLanguage: The internet needs to: deliver messages fast, support thousands of groups changing constantly, let everyone be both sender and receiver, share reserved bandwidth, choose when to be fast or reliable, and keep secrets.

sections.title: Protocol Gaps and Needed Solutions
sections.content:
The RFC identifies eight specific gaps in the Internet protocol suite:

Large-scale resource reservation: RSVP does not support aggregation of reservations for groups of flows, limiting scalability.

IP multicast over ATM: IP multicast cannot take advantage of ATM's multicast capability beyond a single Logical IP Subnet.

Hybrid best-effort and reliable multicast: TCP is unicast only; reliable multicast attempts have struggled with acknowledgment congestion, and no single solution exists.

Network management: A standard distributed simulation MIB format is needed to integrate simulation management with network management via SNMP.

Session protocol: A protocol for starting, pausing, and stopping large exercises is needed; the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) shows promise.

Integrated security: IPv6 security architecture may address this need.

Low-latency naming service: DNS is too slow for rapid multicast group changes; a sub-second group naming and join is needed.

Inter-domain multicast routing: Border Gateway Multicast Protocol (BGMP) shows promise for supporting multicast across multiple providers.
sections.plainLanguage: The gaps are: RSVP doesn't save bandwidth well, ATM isn't used for multicast, reliable multicast is broken, management tools are missing, starting/stopping isn't defined, security is weak, naming is too slow, and providers can't talk to each other about multicast.
